hook.text: The English word father, Latin pater, and Sanskrit pitar all come from one ancient root. Sound shifts left clues.

buildup.text: Historical linguistics traces how languages change over time using regular sound shifts and word comparisons.

discovery.text: Grimm's Law explained systematic consonant shifts from Proto-Indo-European to Germanic languages — like p to f.

twist.text: Languages change constantly but so slowly that speakers rarely notice. Each generation thinks its speech is stable.

climax.text: Historical linguistics reveals that every language alive today is a slow-motion transformation of something older.

punchline.text: Every word carries the ghost of its ancestor.

quiz.question: What does Grimm's Law describe?
options: Systematic consonant shifts between language families

details.summary: Historical linguistics reconstructs how languages change over time through sound shifts, grammatical evolution, and vocabulary replacement. By comparing related languages, researchers reconstruct extinct proto-languages and trace changes spanning thousands of years.
details.whyItMatters: Historical linguistics reveals that language change is constant, systematic, and inevitable. Understanding this process explains why languages diversify and provides tools for reconstructing human prehistory.
takeaways: Languages change systematically through sound shifts and grammatical evolution
Comparative method reconstructs extinct ancestor languages
Language change is constant, inevitable, and follows regular patterns

faq.question: How far back can linguists reconstruct languages?
faq.answer: The comparative method reliably reconstructs languages back roughly 6,000 to 8,000 years. Beyond that, regular sound changes obscure relationships. Proto-Indo-European, spoken around 4500 BCE, is among the best-reconstructed proto-languages.

faq.question: Why do languages change over time?
faq.answer: Children imperfectly replicate adult speech, creating subtle shifts across generations. Contact with other languages introduces borrowings. Social factors like prestige and identity drive adoption of new forms. No language has ever been documented remaining unchanged.
